entries.name: mcp__cmux-cua__get_window_state
entries.description:
Walk a running app's AX tree and return BOTH a structured `elements` array (preferred) AND a Markdown rendering of the same tree (back-compat). Every actionable element is tagged with [element_index N] in the markdown and as `element_index` in the structured array — pass those indices to click, type_text, press_key, etc.

INVARIANT: call get_window_state once per turn per (pid, window_id) before any element-indexed action. The index map is replaced by the next snapshot.

PREFERRED CONSUMERS read `structuredContent.elements` (actionable rows carry `element_index` + `element_token`; value-bearing read-only AXStaticText/AXTextField/AXTextArea rows are also included without addressability fields). Each entry carries `role`, title-first `label`, optional `description` when distinct from the label, `value` (stringified AXValue, capped at 512 characters), `frame: {x,y,w,h}`, `parent_index`, and `depth`. Mirrored actionable AX copies with the same role + label + frame are deduplicated so label lookup is unambiguous. The markdown `tree_markdown` stays available and unchanged in shape for existing text-parsing callers — but new fields will only be added to the structured side.

Always returns BOTH the element tree AND a screenshot — ground on both and cross-check (the tree lies on some surfaces: Electron echo-confirms, Catalyst null values, virtualized off-viewport rows with `h:1` frames). You choose the modality at ACTION time, not here: an element ax action (pass `element_index`/`element_token` → the accessibility rung) or an element px action (pass `x`,`y` → the pixel rung, read straight off this screenshot). `capture_mode` is deprecated and ignored. Pass `include_screenshot:false` to skip the grab and get the tree only — the cheap path when you're just re-indexing before an element ax action.

Optional `query` filters the tree_markdown to matching lines plus their ancestor chain (case-insensitive substring). The element_index values are unchanged — filtering only trims the rendered Markdown.

Optional `max_elements` / … [truncated]

capture_mode.description: DEPRECATED and ignored. get_window_state always returns BOTH the element tree and a screenshot — ground on both. The modality is chosen at action time by how you address the target: an element ax action (element_index/element_token) or an element px action (x,y). Any value (including the old "som"/"screenshot" aliases) is accepted but has no effect.

include_screenshot.description: Default true — returns a grounding screenshot alongside the tree. Set false to skip the grab and return the tree only (the cheap path when you're just re-indexing before an element ax action; saves the image tokens + screen-grab latency). screenshot_out_file still forces a capture to disk.

max_depth.description: Cap on the AX-tree walk depth. Nodes whose rendered indent would exceed this are omitted. Omit for the default (25). Lower this for deep menu/Electron trees.

max_elements.description: Cap on the total number of AX nodes walked. Truncates depth-first; markdown and structured elements truncate together. Omit for the default (2 000). Lower this for Electron / Obsidian / large web apps that produce 10k+ element trees and blow context windows.

screenshot_out_file.description: When set, write the PNG to this file path (~ expanded) instead of embedding base64 in the response. The structured output will contain screenshot_file_path instead.

session.description: Optional explicit session id for the agent cursor and per-session state. Embedded MCP calls may omit it to use CMUX_CUA_DEFAULT_SESSION (or embedded-<pid>); anonymous non-embedded calls remain cursor-less.

window_id.description: Target window ID from list_windows.

entries.name: mcp__cmux-cua__list_apps
entries.description:
List macOS apps — both currently running and installed-but-not-running — with per-app state flags:

- running: is a process for this app live? (pid is 0 when false)
- active: is it the system-frontmost app? (implies running)
- launch_path: filesystem path to the `.app` bundle, when known. Pass this to `launch_app` to start the app cold.
- kind: `"desktop"` for `.app` bundles on macOS.
- last_used: RFC3339 timestamp from the bundle's filesystem mtime, when readable; otherwise null.

Only apps with NSApplicationActivationPolicyRegular are included — background helpers and system UI agents are filtered out. Installed apps come from scanning /Applications, /Applications/Utilities, ~/Applications, /System/Applications, and /System/Applications/Utilities.

Use this for "is X installed?" as well as "is X running?". For per-window state — on-screen, on-current-Space, minimized, window titles — call list_windows instead. For just opening an app — running or not — call launch_app({bundle_id: ...}) directly; list_apps is not a prerequisite.

entries.name: mcp__cmux-cua__list_windows
entries.description:
List all layer-0 top-level windows currently known to WindowServer. Includes off-screen windows (minimized, on another Space, hidden-launched). Use this to find a window_id before calling get_window_state.

Per-record fields: window_id, pid, app_name, title, bounds (x/y/width/height, top-left origin), z_index (higher = frontmost), is_on_screen, on_current_space.

on_screen_only.description: When true, drop windows not on the current Space. Default false.

pid.description: Optional pid filter. When set, only this pid's windows are returned.

S2a: the commands' logic moves into bastion_server::api, with one event bus

Each command's body moves into bastion_server::api::<resource>, taking
plain references where it took Tauri state. The Tauri commands become
one-line calls to it until S3 removes them. A Server holds the engine,
the machine, the factory and a Bus of numbered changes (Change in
bastion-protocol) that keeps the latest 256 for a reconnect to replay.
The factory, the engine watcher and the console publish to the bus, and
the app bridges each change to the Tauri event the page listens for.
EOF
git log --oneline -1

aiTitle: Picking up where we left off

content.text:
S2 is done. It's in two commits: de6861c moved the command logic into the server, and 62ea1a5 adds the API, the event stream and the binary. Neither is pushed.

**What's built:**
- **`bastion_server::api`** holds each command's logic now. The Tauri commands are one-line calls into it until S3 removes them.
- **One event bus** carries every change: jobs, the engine link and console changes. It numbers each change and keeps the latest 256, so a reconnect can catch up. The app forwards each change to the window as the Tauri event the page listens for today.
- **The HTTP API** has one route per action, and every request needs the bearer token. CORS allows only the window's origins.
  - Errors come back as JSON: 400 for a refused action, 409 for the stack's typed refusal, 503 while the factory waits for the engine, and 401 without the token.
- **`GET /events`** streams changes as SSE. It replays what a reconnect missed after `Last-Event-ID`, or sends `resync` when it can't.
- **The `bastion-server` binary** takes `--checkout`, `--data`, `--port` and `--engine`. It keeps its token in `data/token`, readable only by you. It starts or attaches to the stack, starts the factory, and serves on `127.0.0.1`.

**Live check, against the second stack, not your real data:**
- The server started the stack, and the store opened on the third try, once the database worker had registered.
- **Migration 1 ran through the real database worker for the first time.** `user_version` is now 1, and the 5 seeded rules and 3 grants are in place. That database was new; the earlier copy of your real one is still the only run that carried old rows forward.
- A request without the token got 401, and `/engine`, `/jobs` and `/constraints` answered.
- Setting a preset pushed a change on the event stream, a stale `Last-Event-ID` got `resync`, and a bad preset got 400.
- `/stack/stop` stopped the stack.

**Checks:** fmt and clippy are clean. 77 server, 3 app, 86 core and 2 view tests pass. The seam check and the CodeScene gate pass.

**Not checked:**
- **The window with the bridge:** I opened the window once, but the page's content doesn't show in the accessibility tree, so I couldn't confirm the bridge reaches the page.
- **The server on your real stack:** before that, back up your database (`cp data/bastion.db data/bastion.db.bak`). The first start migrates it.

Next is S3: the page calls the server over HTTP and follows `/events`, the Tauri commands go, and the app starts the local server itself.

content.text:
S3 moves the page onto the server. My approach:

- **Command table:** `src/ipc.rs` keeps its shape, `call(command, args)` and `listen(event, ...)`. Instead of `invoke`, it looks the command up in a table of HTTP method and path, and sends the request with the token. The pages barely change.
- **Events:** `listen` follows `GET /events` (the N12 spike's reader) and hands each change to the same event names as before.
- **What the app keeps:** a `target` command that gives the page the local server's URL and token, the quit flow, and starting `bastion-server` as a child process. It stops linking the server crate.

First I'll check how the pages call commands, to build the table.

content.text: Leptos's `on_cleanup` needs a `Send` closure, so the page's open flag goes back to `Arc<AtomicBool>`, as the old `listen` had it.

input.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
p='src/ipc.rs'
s=open(p).read()
def rep(a,b,n=1):
    global s
    assert s.count(a)==n, (a[:50], s.count(a))
    s=s.replace(a,b)
rep("use std::cell::{Cell, RefCell};\nuse std::rc::Rc;","use std::cell::{Cell, RefCell};\nuse std::rc::Rc;\nuse std::sync::Arc;\nuse std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering};")
rep("static LISTENERS: RefCell<Vec<(&'static str, Handler, Rc<Cell<bool>>)>> =","static LISTENERS: RefCell<Vec<(&'static str, Handler, Arc<AtomicBool>)>> =")
rep("""    let open = Rc::new(Cell::new(true));
    let closed = open.clone();
    leptos::prelude::on_cleanup(move || closed.set(false));""","""    let open = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(true));
    let closed = open.clone();
    leptos::prelude::on_cleanup(move || closed.store(false, Ordering::Relaxed));""")
rep("        l.retain(|(_, _, open)| open.get());","        l.retain(|(_, _, open)| open.load(Ordering::Relaxed));")
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
cargo build -p bastion-ui --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -q 2>&1 | grep -E "^(error|warning)" -A6 | grep -E "^(error|warning)|-->" | paste - - | head

entries.name: mcp__cmux-cua__end_session
entries.description: End a session declared with `start_session`: removes its agent cursor, stops any recording it owns, and clears its per-session config. Call this when a run finishes so its cursor doesn't linger (otherwise the idle-TTL reclaims it after a period of inactivity). Idempotent.

session.description: The session id to end.

entries.name: mcp__cmux-cua__start_session
entries.description: Declare a session — a named, color-coded identity for THIS agent run. Pass a stable `session` id; the agent cursor, per-session config, and recording all key on it, and it follows the run across any apps/windows. The cursor's color is derived from the id, so distinct runs are visually distinct. A cursor is shown only for a declared session — call this (or pass `session` on your first action) to opt in. Idempotent: re-calling with the same id just refreshes its idle-TTL. End it with `end_session` (or let the idle-TTL reclaim it). Concurrent runs/subagents each pass their own `session` to get their own cursor.

session.description: Stable session id for this run (e.g. "research-run-1").

entries.name: mcp__cmux-cua__click
entries.description:
Click against a target pid. **Prefer `element_index` over pixel coordinates** — element_index works on backgrounded / minimized / hidden / off-Space windows, surfaces a stable handle that survives rebuilds, and tells you what you're clicking via the cached element's role + label. Reach for `x, y` only when the target is a canvas / video / WebGL / custom-drawn surface that doesn't appear in the AX tree.

Two addressing modes:

- element_index + window_id (from last get_window_state): AX action path. Works on backgrounded/hidden windows. No cursor move, no focus steal. element_index cache is scoped per (pid, window_id) and is replaced by the next snapshot of the same window — re-snapshot every turn before clicking.

- x, y (window-local screenshot pixels, top-left origin of the PNG returned by get_window_state): CGEvent path. Synthesizes mouse events and posts to pid. Before a background post with pid+window_id, the driver checks the front-to-back WindowServer stack and returns error=`obstructed`, code=`background_occluded` without posting if another app/window owns that point. Use modifier for cmd/shift/option/ctrl. Needs a visible on-screen window to anchor the conversion.

button: "left" (default), "right", or "middle". Defaults to left so the field is fully back-compat — omit it and you get the legacy left-click behaviour. Pixel path: routes through the CGEvent left/right/middle mouse-button primitives. AX path: "right" maps to AXShowMenu (same surface as the dedicated `right_click` tool); "middle" has no AX equivalent and falls back to a pixel middle-click at the element's center.
action: press (default), show_menu, pick, confirm, cancel, open.
from_zoom: set true after a zoom call to auto-translate zoom-image pixel coordinates to full-window space.

action.description: AX action: press, show_menu, pick, confirm, cancel, open.

button.description: Mouse button. Default: "left" — omit for legacy left-click behaviour. Pixel path uses the matching CGEvent primitive; AX path maps "right" to AXShowMenu and falls back to a pixel middle-click at the element's center for "middle".

debug_image_out.description: Optional file path. When set on a pixel-addressed click, captures a fresh screenshot, draws a red crosshair at (x, y), and writes the PNG. Use to verify coordinate spaces. Requires window_id; incompatible with from_zoom.

delivery_mode.description: Best-effort-background ladder rung (default "background"). "background": perform the AX action or post the CGEvent without fronting; pixel dispatch with pid+window_id fails with structured error="obstructed", code="background_occluded" when a different visible window owns the screen point. "foreground": briefly front the window, act, let transient UI settle, then restore the prior frontmost app; foreground skips the obstruction check because fronting resolves Z order. Requires window_id. A click that is dispatched remains verified:false — confirm its effect via get_window_state.

element_index.description: Element index from last get_window_state. REQUIRES `pid` and `window_id` to be passed alongside it — element_index alone (no pid) fails fast with "Missing required integer field: pid"; it is not a silent no-op.

element_token.description: Opaque per-snapshot element handle from `structuredContent.elements[].element_token` of the last get_window_state. Takes precedence over element_index when both supplied. Returns an explicit "stale" error if the snapshot has been superseded — re-snapshot in that case.

from_zoom.description: When true, x and y are in the last zoom image for this pid; driver translates back to full-window coordinates.

modifier.description: Modifier keys: cmd, shift, option/alt, ctrl.

scope.description: Coordinate frame for a windowless screen-absolute click (default "window"). Pass "desktop" when sending x,y with NO pid/window_id — the coordinates are then true screen pixels (read from get_desktop_state with scope="desktop"). Per-call; not a setting.

session.description: Optional explicit session id for the agent cursor and per-session state. Embedded MCP calls may omit it to use CMUX_CUA_DEFAULT_SESSION (or embedded-<pid>); anonymous non-embedded calls remain cursor-less.

window_id.description: Target window ID. Required for element_index. Optional when element_token is supplied (the token carries it).

x.description: X in screenshot pixels, read straight off the image you were handed — no scaling math needed. With pid+window_id (capture_scope=window): window-local pixels from the get_window_state PNG (top-left origin). Windowless (no pid/window_id, capture_scope=desktop): pixels from the get_desktop_state PNG (the native full-display image). Either way, the pixel you read IS the pixel that gets clicked; the driver undoes the Retina backing scale + any downscale internally.

y.description: Y in screenshot pixels (see x). Window-local from get_window_state, or full-display from get_desktop_state under capture_scope=desktop.

entries.name: mcp__cmux-cua__hotkey
entries.description:
Press a key combination — e.g. `["cmd", "c"]` for Copy, `["cmd", "shift", "4"]` for screenshot selection. Follows the same `delivery_mode` ladder as click/type_text — it does NOT raise the window by default:
• `background` (default): post the combo to the target pid WITHOUT fronting or raising it — uses the macOS 14+ auth-message envelope so Chromium/Electron accept it as trusted live input. No focus steal. `window_id` here only targets the combo; it does not raise.
• `foreground`: briefly front the window (NSMenu path, < 1 ms via SLPSSetFrontProcessWithOptions) so native menu key-equivalents (Cmd+Z, Cmd+W) dispatch, then restore the prior frontmost — the explicit escalation for menu-bar shortcuts on non-Chromium apps that ignore a background combo. Requires window_id.

A combo is never driver-verifiable (no read-back) → effect:"unverifiable"; confirm via screenshot. NOTE: a keyboard combo does NOT focus a text field — to type into a backgrounded Electron input, establish real renderer focus with a PIXEL click first, then `type_text` (do not reach for a clipboard + Cmd+V dance).

Recognized modifiers: cmd/command, shift, option/alt, ctrl/control, fn. Non-modifier keys use the same vocabulary as `press_key`. Order: modifiers first, one non-modifier last.

delivery_mode.description: Best-effort-background ladder rung (default "background"). "background": inject without fronting or raising the target — no focus steal. "foreground": briefly front the target, act, then restore the prior frontmost — the explicit last resort when a background attempt didn't land. Re-call with "foreground" only for the action that needs it.

keys.description: Modifier(s) and one non-modifier key, e.g. ["cmd", "c"].

session.description: Optional explicit session id for the agent cursor and per-session state. Embedded MCP calls may omit it to use CMUX_CUA_DEFAULT_SESSION (or embedded-<pid>); anonymous non-embedded calls remain cursor-less.

window_id.description: Target window. Required for delivery_mode:"foreground" (the NSMenu activation needs a window). Does NOT itself raise the window — raising is gated on delivery_mode.

x.description: Screenshot-pixel X — the element px action form: pixel-click there to focus, then send the combo (so e.g. Cmd+V pastes into that field). Pass with y. Use for Chromium/Electron surfaces the background combo can't reach.

entries.name: mcp__cmux-cua__bring_to_front
entries.description: Persistently activate an app so it genuinely holds macOS foreground, then leave it there. Most input does NOT need this — every macOS dispatch reaches backgrounded windows, and `dispatch:"foreground"` does its own brief front→act→restore. Reach for `bring_to_front` only for a focus-proxy surface that re-arms its own input channel on activation and must stay frontmost across the interaction — chiefly a remote-desktop client (Microsoft Windows App / RDP), where the brief flash drops keystrokes. Activates the owning app by pid (`NSRunningApplication.activate`); `window_id` is accepted for parity but activation is app-level. p='PLAN.md'; s=open(p).read()

    s=s.replace(a,b)

s=s[:i]+"""| D30 | The app keeps a list of Bastion servers the owner added, each a name, a base URL and a token kept in the Keychain. The server the app starts on this machine is `local`. Each job runs on one server: New request picks it from that list, `local` by default, and the job page names it. Every server stays connected, and the Jobs page lists the jobs of all of them. The sidebar names no server. Replaces D12's profiles. | The owner's choice (2026-11-06), replacing a target per workspace: use several backends at once, chosen job by job. |"""+s[j:]
rep("""- **S4, targets.** The target list, the local target started by the app,
  workspaces from every target in one list, and each workspace's pages on its
  own target.""","""- **S4, servers.** The list of servers in Settings, `local` started by the
  app, a server picker on New request that defaults to `local`, the server's
  name on the job page, and the Jobs page listing every server's jobs.""")
rep("""**Exit, live:** with two targets connected (a second stack on this machine),
a workspace on each runs a job.""","""**Exit, live:** with two servers connected (`local`, and a second stack on
this machine), a job runs on each, picked on New request.""")
rep(""" 86 core, 77 server, 3 app tests. Next: S3, the view on the API. |""",""" 86 core, 77 server, 3 app tests (62ea1a5). S3, the view on the API: the page sends each server command over HTTP by a route table in `bastion-protocol` (a server test sends every row and fails on a 404 or 405), with the token from the window's `target` command, and follows `GET /events` with `fetch`, reconnecting with `Last-Event-ID`; a resync, a reconnect or the window's focus makes every page read again, the engine status included. The app keeps three commands (`profile`, `target`, `quit`), no longer links the server, and starts `bastion-server` in its own process group, or attaches to the one on port 49190. The page decides a quit: it asks only while the stack runs, and the server outlives the app. Live (2026-11-06), on the owner's stack after backing up `data/bastion.db`: the app started the local server, migration 1 ran through the `database` worker and kept the 15 jobs and 83 artifacts; the Jobs page showed them and the Engine page the link up; with the server killed the Link card said `Down: http://127.0.0.1:49190 does not answer.`, and after a restart the open page came back up with no reload; a relaunched app attached to the running server instead of starting another. Not confirmed: the quit question (the window rendered blank to the screen reader after its close button), and ⌘Q quits without asking, as Tauri's Quit menu item exits with a code; a stale error stays on the stack card after an outage. The sidebar's server label is gone (D30). 86 core, 78 server, 3 app, 3 view, 1 protocol tests. Next: S4, servers. |""")
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

lines: | D27 | Bastion is a server and its clients. `bastion-server`, one Rust binary on `axum` and `tokio`, is the source of truth: it holds the factory (`bastion-core` and its adapter), the store, the gate, the audit chain, the forge, and the stack on its machine. Business logic lives in the server; iii workers are the implementation under it, reached only through the Engine seam. A client shows state, sends the owner's actions and follows updates, and keeps no business state. Replaces D18's "in the app", D13's app-owned stack, and §10's second adapter. | The owner's choice (2026-11-06). Jobs advance with no app open, and one server serves the app on this machine or another. D18 kept the core pure, so it moves without change. |

| D28 | The API is HTTP with JSON. Each route is one action on one resource, its types live in `bastion-protocol`, and every request carries the target's bearer token. The view calls the server from the webview. Replaces D9's Tauri commands, except the few that belong to the window (S3). | One surface for every client, typed once. |

| D29 | Push is server-sent events. `GET /events` streams D10's `{kind, id, revision}` with an event id. A client that reconnects with `Last-Event-ID` gets what it missed, or a `resync` when it is too far behind, and then reads again. The view reads the stream with `fetch`, so the token goes in a header. WebSockets wait until a client must stream to the server, such as a live terminal. | Push is one-way today. SSE is plain HTTP, so it passes the same token, proxy and SSH tunnel as the API. |

-| D30 | The app connects to API targets. A target is a name, a base URL and a token kept in the Keychain. Every target stays connected at once. A workspace lives on one target, because its server owns its records; the app lists the workspaces of every target, and a page about a workspace or its jobs talks to that workspace's target. The local target is a server the app starts on this machine. Replaces D12's profiles. | The owner's choice (2026-11-06): use several backends at once, with each workspace on its own target. |

+| D30 | The app keeps a list of Bastion servers the owner added, each a name, a base URL and a token kept in the Keychain. The server the app starts on this machine is `local`. Each job runs on one server: New request picks it from that list, `local` by default, and the job page names it. Every server stays connected, and the Jobs page lists the jobs of all of them. | A6 | done | Spike N9: `judge::evaluate` has no provider worker in this stack, so a run is graded by a harness turn with no tools; `harness::metrics` meters each session (docs/levels.md). The `bastion-server` binary takes `--checkout`, `--data`, `--port` and `--engine`, keeps its token in `data/token` (mode 0600), starts or attaches to the stack, and serves on loopback. Live (2026-11-06) against the second stack: the server started the stack, opened the store on the third try once `database` registered, ran migration 1 through the worker (`user_version` 1, the seed's 5 constraints and 3 grants), refused a request with no token, answered `/engine`, `/jobs` and `/constraints`, pushed a change on `/events` when a preset was set, answered a stale `Last-Event-ID` with `resync`, refused a bad preset with 400, and stopped the stack through `/stack/stop`. 86 core, 77 server, 3 app tests (62ea1a5). S3, the view on the API: the page sends each server command over HTTP by a route table in `bastion-protocol` (a server test sends every row and fails on a 404 or 405), with the token from the window's `target` command, and follows `GET /events` with `fetch`, reconnecting with `Last-Event-ID`; a resync, a reconnect or the window's focus makes every page read again, the engine status included. The app keeps three commands (`profile`, `target`, `quit`), no longer links the server, and starts `bastion-server` in its own process group, or attaches to the one on port 49190. The page decides a quit: it asks only while the stack runs, and the server outlives the app. Live (2026-11-06), on the owner's stack after backing up `data/bastion.db`: the app started the local server, migration 1 ran through the `database` worker and kept the 15 jobs and 83 artifacts; the Jobs page showed them and the Engine page the link up; with the server killed the Link card said `Down: http://127.0.0.1:49190 does not answer.`, and after a restart the open page came back up with no reload; a relaunched app attached to the running server instead of starting another. Not confirmed: the quit question (after its close button, screenshots of the window came back blank), and ⌘Q quits without asking, as Tauri's Quit menu item exits with a code; a stale error stays on the stack card after an outage. The sidebar's server label is gone (D30). 86 core, 78 server, 3 app, 3 view, 1 protocol tests. Next: S4, servers. |

git status --short | head -20; git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
S3: the page talks to its server over HTTP and follows its events

The page sends each server command over HTTP by a route table in
bastion-protocol, which a server test checks row by row, using the token
from the window's `target` command. It follows GET /events with fetch,
reconnecting with Last-Event-ID; a resync, a reconnect or focus makes
every page read again. While the server cannot be reached, the engine
shows as down.

The app keeps three commands (profile, target, quit), no longer links the
server, and starts bastion-server in its own process group or attaches to
the one already listening, so jobs go on after the app quits. The page
decides a quit and asks only while the stack runs. The sidebar no longer
names a server; each job will pick one (D30, S4).
EOF
git log --oneline -1

content.text:
S3 is committed (8004bb8) and not pushed. I also removed the "this machine" label from the sidebar. The per-job server picker lands in S4, and D30 and S4 in the plan now say each job picks its server, defaulting to `local`.

**What changed:**
- The page sends every server command over HTTP with the token, and follows `/events` for live updates.
- The route table lives in `bastion-protocol`, and a server test sends every route, so a typo fails the build instead of returning 404.
- The app has three commands left (`profile`, `target`, `quit`) and no longer contains the server.
- The app starts `bastion-server` as its own process, or attaches to one already running, so jobs keep going after you quit the app.

**Seen working in the window, on your real stack:**
- **Your database was migrated.** I backed it up first, to `data/bastion.db.bak-2026-11-06`. Migration 1 ran through the database worker, and all 15 jobs and 83 artifacts are still there.
- The Jobs page listed the 15 jobs, and the Engine page showed the link up.
- I killed the server. The Link card said "Down: http://127.0.0.1:49190 does not answer."
- I restarted the server. The open page came back up without a reload.
- I relaunched the app. It attached to the running server instead of starting a second one.

**Not working or not confirmed:**
- **⌘Q quits without asking.** Tauri's built-in Quit menu item exits directly, which I think predates S3. The A1 check only tested closing the window.
- **Closing the window:** the app stayed open, but screenshots of the window came back blank, so I couldn't see the question.
- **A stale error:** after an outage, the "cannot be reached" message stays on the Stack card until you act on it.

Checks: fmt and clippy are clean, the seam check passes, and 171 tests pass (86 core, 78 server, 3 app, 3 page, 1 protocol). The CodeScene gate passes. I stopped the stack and the server afterward.

One question before S4. A job runs on the server you pick, but each workspace points at a repository path on one machine. When a job picks a server, should the list of workspaces come from that server, so each server keeps its own? Or should a workspace be defined once and exist on every server, which means each server needs its own copy of the repository?

questions.question: Today a workspace is one repository (name, path on disk, branch), and one server can hold several. When you say each server IS its own workspace, which do you mean?

options.label: One server, one repo
options.description: A Bastion server is set up for exactly one repository: its path and branch are server settings (flags or Settings). The workspaces table, the Add workspace form and the workspace filter go away. To work on another repo, add another Bastion server (a second stack). A job's server choice also picks its repo.
options.preview:
New request
  Bastion server: [ local (bastion, main) v ]
  Request: ...

Settings
  Bastion servers
    local    http://127.0.0.1:49190  repo ~/tacoda/bastion @ main
    box      http://...              repo ~/src/app @ main

options.label: Rename only
options.description: Keep the model: a server still holds several repositories. Only the words change: drop "workspace" from the page, so the list of repos lives under each Bastion server, and a job picks a Bastion server and then one of its repos.

What would you like to clarify? The fork is this:

1. **One server, one repository.** Each Bastion server is set up for exactly one repository. Workspaces go away entirely, and picking a server on New request also picks the repository.

content.text:
Understood. A Bastion server holds several workspaces, one per repository, and each workspace will carry its own setup, checks and testing. The word "target" goes everywhere, and "profile" leaves the page; the thing is a **Bastion server**.

The pages besides Jobs and New request (Engine, Settings, Constraints, Capabilities, Audit, Evals) each describe one server. My assumption: each of those pages gets a server picker at the top, defaulting to `local`. The choice carries across pages, and nothing about servers goes in the sidebar.

S4 in four steps:
1. **S4a, the server list in the app:** `local` comes first. You can add more, each with a name, URL and token, and the token is kept in the macOS Keychain. The commands become `servers`, `server_add` and `server_remove`, replacing `target`.
2. **S4b, the page client on many servers:** every call names its server, and the page follows one event stream per server.
3. **S4c, jobs:** the Jobs page lists the jobs of every server. New request picks a server (default `local`), then one of that server's workspaces. The job page names its server.
4. **S4d, the per-server pages:** the picker, then the live exit with the second stack.

Recording the decision and the terminology first.

---
name: bastion-server-terminology
description: In Bastion, a backend is a "Bastion server" — never "target" or "profile"; each server holds workspaces, one per repo
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Call a Bastion backend a **Bastion server** in code, UI and docs. Do not use "target" or "profile" for it (the owner rejected the double terminology, 2026-11-06). A Bastion server holds several workspaces, one per repository, each with its own setup, checks and tests. Each job picks its server on New request (`local` by default); per-server pages get a picker at the top, never a sidebar label.

**Why:** two words for one thing confused the owner; a workspace is the per-repo unit and differs per project.

**How to apply:** when naming types, commands, routes or labels for backends, use `server`/`Bastion server`; reserve "workspace" for a repository on a server. See [[bastion-rust-app]].

content.text:
### Set, get, and delete a password with keyring::Entry

Source: https://github.com/open-source-cooperative/keyring-rs/blob/v3.6.3/README.md

Create an entry with Entry::new, set a password, retrieve it, and delete the credential. The example prints the password and returns Ok(()) on success.

```rust
use keyring::{Entry, Result};

fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let entry = Entry::new("my-service", "my-name")?;
    entry.set_password("topS3cr3tP4$$w0rd")?;
    let password = entry.get_password()?;
    println!("My password is '{}'", password);
    entry.delete_credential()?;
    Ok(())
}
```

--------------------------------

### Add keyring dependency with features in Cargo.toml

Source: https://github.com/open-source-cooperative/keyring-rs/blob/v3.6.3/README.md

Include the keyring crate in your project's [dependencies] section, specifying features for each supported credential store. This example enables Apple-native, Windows-native, and synchronous Secret Service stores.

```toml
keyring = { version = "3", features = ["apple-native", "windows-native", "sync-secret-service"] }
```

--------------------------------

### Keyring-rs > Usage

Source: https://github.com/open-source-cooperative/keyring-rs/blob/v3.6.3/README.md

To use this crate in your project, you must include it in your `Cargo.toml` and specify a feature for each supported credential store you want to use. For example, if you want to use the platform credential stores on Mac and Win, and use the Secret Service (synchronously) on Linux and \*nix platforms, you would add a snippet such as this to your `[dependencies]` section:

```toml
keyring = { version = "3", features = ["apple-native", "windows-native", "sync-secret-service"] }
```

This will give you access to the `keyring` crate in your code. Now you can use the `Entry::new` function to create a new keyring entry. The `new` function takes a service name and a user's name which together identify the entry.

Passwords (strings) or secrets (binary data) can be added to an entry using its `set_password` or `set_secret` methods, respectively. (These methods create an entry in the underlying credential store.) The password or secret can then be read back using the `get_password` or `get_secret` methods. The underlying credential (with its password/secret data) can then be removed using the `delete_credential` method.

--------------------------------

### Platforms

Source: https://github.com/open-source-cooperative/keyring-rs/blob/v3.6.3/README.md

## Platforms

This crate provides built-in implementations of the following platform-specific credential stores:

* _Linux_: The DBus-based Secret Service, the kernel keyutils, and a combo of the two.
* _FreeBSD_, _OpenBSD_: The DBus-based Secret Service.
* _macOS_, _iOS_: The local keychain.
* _Windows_: The Windows Credential Manager.

To enable the stores you want, you use features: there is one feature for each possibly-included credential store. If you specify a feature (e.g., `dbus-secret-service`) _and_ your target platform (e.g., `freebsd`) supports that credential store, it will be included as the default credential store in that build. That way you can have a build command that specifies a single credential store for each of your target platforms, and use that same build command for all targets.

If you don't enable any credential stores that are supported on a given platform, the _mock_ keystore will be the default on that platform. See the [developer docs](https://docs.rs/keyring/) for details of which features control the inclusion of which credential stores.

--------------------------------

### Upgrading from v2

Source: https://github.com/open-source-cooperative/keyring-rs/blob/v3.6.3/README.md

## Upgrading from v2

The major functional change between v2 and v3 is the addition of synchronous support for the Secret Service via the [dbus-secret-service crate](https://crates.io/crates/dbus-secret-service). This means that keyring users of the Secret Service no longer need to link with an async runtime. (There are other advantages as well; see [above](#platform-specific-issues) for details.)

The main API change between v2 and v3 is the addition of support for non-string (i.e., binary) "password" data. To accommodate this, two changes have been made:

1. There are two new methods on `Entry` objects: `set_secret` and `get_secret`. These are the analogs of `set_password` and `get_password`, but instead of taking or returning strings they take or return binary data (byte arrays/vectors).

2. The v2 method `delete_password` has been renamed `delete_credential`, both to clarify what's actually being deleted and to emphasize that it doesn't matter whether it's holding a "password" or a "secret".

Another API change between v2 and v3 is that the notion of a default feature set has gone away: you must now specify explicitly which crate-supported keystores you want included (other than the `mock` keystore, which is always present). So all keyring client developers will need to update their `Cargo.toml` file to use the new features correctly.

All v2 data is fully forward-compatible with v3 data; there have been no changes at all in that respect.

The MSRV has been moved to 1.75, and all direct dependencies are at their latest stable versions.

input.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
p='PLAN.md'; s=open(p).read()
a=" 86 core, 78 server, 3 app, 3 view, 1 protocol tests. Next: S4, servers. |"
assert a in s
s=s.replace(a," 86 core, 78 server, 3 app, 3 view, 1 protocol tests (8004bb8). S4, Bastion servers, built: the app keeps the servers the owner added in `servers.toml`, each token in the Keychain (`keyring`), with `local` always first; the page follows every server's events and calls any of them (`call_on`). The Jobs page lists every server's jobs, each row naming its server, and the filter offers each server and workspace that has jobs. New request picks a Bastion server, `local` by default, then one of its workspaces; opening a job makes its server the current one, and the job page names it. The pages about one server have a Bastion server picker at their top, and Settings lists the servers with add and remove. The `profile` command is gone from the page; `profiles.toml` only tells the app how to start `local`. 86 core, 78 server, 5 app, 3 view, 1 protocol tests. Next: the S exit, live. |")
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
S4: Bastion servers, chosen job by job

The app keeps the Bastion servers the owner added in servers.toml, each
token in the Keychain, with `local` first. The page follows every
server's events and can call any of them. The Jobs page lists every
server's jobs and names each one's server. New request picks a server,
`local` by default, then one of its workspaces; a job's page talks to
its own server and names it. The pages about one server get a server
picker at their top, and Settings lists the servers with add and remove.
The page no longer shows a profile.
EOF
git log --oneline -1

aiTitle: Picking up where we left off

content.text:
S4 is built and committed (fe68813), not pushed. The words now follow your decision: **Bastion server** throughout, with "target" and "profile" gone, and each server holds its own workspaces, one per repository. I saved that terminology as a memory for future sessions.

**What it does:**
- **Choosing a server per job:** New request has a Bastion server picker that starts at `local`, then a workspace picker showing that server's workspaces.
- **Jobs page:** lists the jobs from every server. Each row names its server, and the filter offers each server and workspace that has jobs.
- **Job page:** opening a job switches to its server and shows the server's name as a badge.
- **Pages about one server** (Engine, Settings, Constraints, Capabilities, Audit Log, Evals) have a Bastion server picker at the top, starting at `local`. The sidebar names no server.
- **Settings:** lists the servers and lets you add one (name, URL, token) or remove one. `local` can't be removed. A token is stored in the macOS Keychain, never in `servers.toml`.
- **Live updates:** the page follows every server's event stream. Job changes from any server refresh the Jobs page. Engine and console changes show only from the server you're viewing.
- The page no longer shows a profile; `profiles.toml` only tells the app how to start `local`.

**Checks:** fmt and clippy are clean, the seam check passes, and all tests pass: 86 core, 78 server, 5 app, 3 page and 1 protocol. The CodeScene gate passes.

**Not run yet: the S exit, live.** With two servers connected (`local` and a second stack on this machine), a job would run on each, chosen on New request. That exercises the Keychain add through the page, the merged Jobs list, and the per-server pages. It spends model money: two plan turns on gpt-5-mini, under about $0.05 in total. The second server also needs a workspace added through Settings, such as `demo-a`.

Should I run it?

entries.name: mcp__cmux-cua__type_text
entries.description:
Insert text into the target pid via `AXSetAttribute(kAXSelectedText)`. Works for standard Cocoa text fields and text views. No keystrokes are synthesized — special keys (Return / Escape / arrows) go through `press_key` / `hotkey`. For Chromium / Electron inputs that don't implement `kAXSelectedText`, the tool falls back to CGEvent character synthesis automatically.

Optional `element_index` + `window_id` (from the last `get_window_state` snapshot) directs the write to a specific field. Without `element_index`, the write goes to the pid's currently focused element.

WEB CONTENT (Chromium/WebKit/Electron — browser tabs, Slack, VS Code, X's compose box): the AX layer accepts a write and echoes it back through AXValue while the renderer/DOM never observes it. The driver detects this at the element level (an AXWebArea ancestor) and refuses to trust that echo — an AX-path insert into web content returns effect:"unverifiable" + escalation, never a false "confirmed" (a browser's own native address bar/toolbar stays trusted). For a browser TAB the reliable path is the `page` tool (drives the DOM via CDP); for an embedded web view use this tool's px form: pass x,y (no element_index) to pixel-click the field then type, in one call. NOTE: a px focus-click won't reliably open+focus a CLOSED control; AX-press to open/activate it first (works in the background), then px-type. Always confirm via the screenshot; if px-background still drops, escalate to delivery_mode:"foreground".

delay_ms.description: Milliseconds between characters in the CGEvent fallback path. Default 30. Ignored when the AX path succeeds.

delivery_mode.description: Best-effort-background ladder rung (default "background"). "background": AX insert, then CGEvent keystrokes if needed — no focus steal; the driver verifies via an AXValue read-back and reports `verified`. "foreground": briefly front the window, type, restore the prior frontmost — the explicit last resort for focus-sensitive surfaces (e.g. WhatsApp/Catalyst) where background keystrokes don't land. Re-call with "foreground" when a background attempt returns `verified:false` and a screenshot shows the text didn't appear.

element_index.description: Element index from last get_window_state. Directs the write to a specific field. REQUIRES `pid` and `window_id` to be passed alongside it — element_index alone (no pid) fails fast with "Missing required integer field: pid"; it is not a silent no-op.

element_token.description: Opaque per-snapshot element handle from `structuredContent.elements[].element_token`. Takes precedence over element_index when both supplied. Returns an explicit "stale" error if the snapshot has been superseded.

session.description: Optional explicit session id for the agent cursor and per-session state. Embedded MCP calls may omit it to use CMUX_CUA_DEFAULT_SESSION (or embedded-<pid>); anonymous non-embedded calls remain cursor-less.

text.description: Text to insert at the target's cursor.

window_id.description: CGWindowID. Required when element_index is used. Optional when element_token is supplied (the token carries it).

x.description: Screenshot-pixel X of the field to type into — the element px action form. Pass x,y (no element_index) and the tool pixel-clicks there to establish real renderer focus, then types. Use for Chromium/Electron inputs the AX path can't reach. Read straight off the get_window_state PNG, same convention as click.

y.description: Screenshot-pixel Y of the field (see x).

entries.name: mcp__cmux-cua__press_key
entries.description:
Press and release a single key, delivered to the target pid via CGEventPostToPid. Follows the same `delivery_mode` ladder as click/type_text — it does NOT raise the window by default:
• `background` (default): post to the pid WITHOUT fronting/raising — the auth-message path (Chromium-safe). With element_index it focuses that AX element first. `window_id` only targets; it does not raise.
• `foreground`: briefly front the window (NSMenu path, < 1 ms) so native menu key-equivalents dispatch, then restore prior frontmost — the explicit escalation for menu shortcuts an app drops in the background. Requires window_id (and no element_index).

A key press is never driver-verifiable → effect:"unverifiable"; confirm via screenshot. Key names: return, tab, escape, up/down/left/right, space, delete, home, end, pageup, pagedown, f1-f12, plus any letter or digit. Modifiers array: cmd, shift, option/alt, ctrl, fn.

delivery_mode.description: Best-effort-background ladder rung (default "background"). "background": inject without fronting or raising the target — no focus steal. "foreground": briefly front the target, act, then restore the prior frontmost — the explicit last resort when a background attempt didn't land. Re-call with "foreground" only for the action that needs it.

element_token.description: Opaque per-snapshot element handle from `structuredContent.elements[].element_token`. Takes precedence over element_index when both supplied. Returns an explicit "stale" error if the snapshot has been superseded.

key.description: Key name: return, tab, escape, up, down, etc.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys: cmd, shift, option/alt, ctrl, fn.

session.description: Optional explicit session id for the agent cursor and per-session state. Embedded MCP calls may omit it to use CMUX_CUA_DEFAULT_SESSION (or embedded-<pid>); anonymous non-embedded calls remain cursor-less.

window_id.description: Target window. Required for delivery_mode:"foreground". Does NOT itself raise the window — raising is gated on delivery_mode.

x.description: Screenshot-pixel X — the element px action form: pixel-click there to focus, then send the key. Use when the key must go to a Chromium/Electron surface the AX path can't focus. Pass with y, no element_index.

| A8 | in progress | Spike N11 (20a9b71): the `configuration` worker can carry config as YAML, but the owner chose the database (D26). The Constraints and Capabilities pages each show charter, harness and factory sections (D25, 062cd3e), checked in the window. A7's exit was checked again: pull request #2 merged (2beb204), issue #1 closed, the job's branch deleted, CI green on `main`. D26 (7e22bc3): the defaults moved into `seed/governance.sql`, and the gate reads the database again before each turn. 58 core tests, 67 app tests. Step 1, the graph in the core: every full-pipeline stage with its kind, the full pipeline with and without acceptance tests, a dial per checkpoint with wipp's presets and merge held at least, steps the factory runs (`RunStep`, `StepPassed`, `StepFailed`), the revise loop with wipp's limits and the stop on a repeated failure, and one implement turn per task. Checkpoints stay their own stages (the owner's choice, 2026-11-06), and the agent's review turn is `code_review`. 75 core tests, 67 app tests (2881686). Step 2, shape: scope and discover briefs; discovery's reply read into tasks and questions, and clarify passed when there are none; the clarify checkpoint shows discovery's report and takes the answers as a note; read-only turns tag the VM's `HEAD` first and are reset to it after, so a commit made in one goes too; prepare passes at once (no setup steps until A9); `job_submit` takes a pipeline. The store gained numbered migrations on `user_version`: migration 1 rebuilds `jobs`, `artifacts` and `capabilities` with a stage check from `Stage::ALL` and the new job columns, and adds `tasks` and `revisions` tables (D8). The rebuild keeps the table's name, because with foreign keys on (which the worker may set; not checked), renaming a new table into place fails at commit; both were tried on a copy of `data/bastion.db`, and the generated migration kept its 15 jobs and 83 artifacts. Not yet run through the `database` worker itself. Scope's split verdict is not read until step 6. 79 core tests, 69 app tests (0971e08). Step 3, acceptance tests: define, your checks (approve keeps every criterion, a note redefines, up to 3 times), specify, baseline, falsify, and verify and acceptance as steps the factory runs. The app reads specify's JSON (`src-tauri/src/spec.rs`, so the core stays on `serde` and `sha2`, D19); a reply that does not read is `Outcome::Unusable` and gets one more try. The baseline commits the spec's files, runs each check in the VM (exit 0 is green; 126 and 127 did not run), puts back tracked files the checks wrote, and passes only when every check fails. Checks that pass already go to falsify once per spec: the turn breaks the product code from a tag made before it, the checks run against it, the tree resets to the tag, and a check that stayed green, or a test the turn changed, sends the spec back. A passing baseline tags the tree `bastion-spec`; verify waits on the owner when a spec file differs from the tag, or a check cannot run, and sends an unmet criterion back to implement. Not ported from wipp: layers, Gherkin, lint on the tests, property tests, critical models and strength; they need repository settings Bastion does not have. S3, the view on the API: the page sends each server command over HTTP by a route table in `bastion-protocol` (a server test sends every row and fails on a 404 or 405), with the token from the window's `target` command, and follows `GET /events` with `fetch`, reconnecting with `Last-Event-ID`; a resync, a reconnect or the window's focus makes every page read again, the engine status included. The app keeps three commands (`profile`, `target`, `quit`), no longer links the server, and starts `bastion-server` in its own process group, or attaches to the one on port 49190. The page decides a quit: it asks only while the stack runs, and the server outlives the app. Live (2026-11-06), on the owner's stack after backing up `data/bastion.db`: the app started the local server, migration 1 ran through the `database` worker and kept the 15 jobs and 83 artifacts; the Jobs page showed them and the Engine page the link up; with the server killed the Link card said `Down: http://127.0.0.1:49190 does not answer.`, and after a restart the open page came back up with no reload; a relaunched app attached to the running server instead of starting another. Not confirmed: the quit question (after its close button, screenshots of the window came back blank), and ⌘Q quits without asking, as Tauri's Quit menu item exits with a code; a stale error stays on the stack card after an outage. The sidebar's server label is gone (D30). 86 core, 78 server, 3 app, 3 view, 1 protocol tests (8004bb8). S4, Bastion servers, built: the app keeps the servers the owner added in `servers.toml`, each token in the Keychain (`keyring`), with `local` always first; the page follows every server's events and calls any of them (`call_on`). The Jobs page lists every server's jobs, each row naming its server, and the filter offers each server and workspace that has jobs. New request picks a Bastion server, `local` by default, then one of its workspaces; opening a job makes its server the current one, and the job page names it. The pages about one server have a Bastion server picker at their top, and Settings lists the servers with add and remove. The `profile` command is gone from the page; `profiles.toml` only tells the app how to start `local`. 86 core, 78 server, 5 app, 3 view, 1 protocol tests. Next: the S exit, live. |

aiTitle: Picking up where we left off

content.text:
I ran the S exit live with two Bastion servers, and it mostly passed. It's recorded in the plan and committed (21b7bad), not pushed.

**Worked:**
- **Adding a server:** I added server Two in Settings. Its token went into the Keychain, not into `servers.toml`.
- **Picking a server per job:**
  - New request on `local` with `demo-local` started job `j7df1a6c2`.
  - Picking Two switched the workspace list to Two's `demo-two`, and started `jcbf97e51`.
- **Jobs page:** listed both jobs, each with its server's name. Each ran one plan and stopped at Approve.
- **Quit question:** closing the window with the stack running asked the question, which S3 couldn't confirm. "Keep it running" quit the app and left both servers and both stacks running.
- **Reopen:** the relaunched app showed both jobs where they were.
- **Killing only a server:** killing just Two's server process left its stack running. The restarted server attached to the same stack.

**Found, still open:**
- **The Jobs page doesn't notice a dead server.** While Two's server was down, its job still showed as running, from the last read.
- **A waiting job loses its VM if its stack restarts.** My first kill also took Two's stack down. Its job, waiting at Approve, lost its VM, so approving it would have failed.
- **A kill mid-turn wasn't really tested.** The plan finished too fast to tell whether it survived the kill.
- **Small:** macOS capitalized "two" to "Two", and the add-server form keeps its values after Add.

**Cost:** two plan turns on gpt-5-mini. I didn't measure the exact spend.

**State now:** I stopped both test jobs and both stacks. The local server is still running, which is how the design intends it.

Next in the plan: make the Jobs page show when a server can't be reached, then go back to A8 step 4. The lost VM matters more for a real job; I'd fix it during A8, since revive is part of A8 step 5. Should I start with the Jobs page fix?

python3 - <<'EOF'
p='PLAN.md'; s=open(p).read()
a=" the add-server form keeps its values after Add. Next: fix the Jobs page's unreachable server, then A8 step 4. |"
assert a in s
s=s.replace(a," the add-server form keeps its values after Add. Then the Jobs page's unreachable server: the page now marks a server whose event stream is down, names it above the list, keeps that server's jobs as last read and marks them unreachable, and still says why a reachable server's jobs did not read; checked live by killing only Two's server, which put up the note, and restarting it, which cleared the note and brought Two's job back with no reload. Next: A8 step 4. |")
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
The Jobs page says when a Bastion server cannot be reached

Each server's event feed records whether it answers. While a server is
down, the Jobs page names it, keeps its jobs as last read and marks them
unreachable; a reachable server whose jobs did not read still says why.
On reconnect the note clears and the page reads again.
EOF
git log --oneline -1

lines: | A6 | done | Spike N9: `judge::evaluate` has no provider worker in this stack, so a run is graded by a harness turn with no tools; `harness::metrics` meters each session (docs/levels.md). Build (38519c5): `Dials::trial` in the core (a trial approves its own plan and stops at review with its diff, so nothing lands), the core's `eval` module (arms, tally from the audit, totals, differences, grade), an arm's rungs applied per trial job in the gate, every turn of every job metered into `turns`, the eval tables, and the Evals page. 51 core tests, 58 app tests. Live exit (2026-10-31), eval `ee8eaaddd` on `demo-a` from `d6227b2`: three requests that each ask for a `wc` count, A with `no-wc` told and B with it enforced. All six runs reached review and were graded. In total B differs from A: refused 0 -> 5, review findings 2 -> 0, turns 39 -> 28, calls 33 -> 17, cost $0.0344 -> $0.0207; grades 7 and 7. Each request lists B's refused calls with their audit entries (#375, #405, #363, #452, ...) and links to the trial job, which shows it stopped at review with Land pending. Apply B set `no-wc` to enforced and the audit recorded `ee8eaaddd arm b: Told -> Enforced` (#487) and the eval the owner acted on (#488). Not varied yet: the model per stage and the pipeline, since there is one of each until A7 and A8. |

content.text:
I pushed 21b7bad, and the Jobs page fix is committed as 63eb225 (not pushed).

**What it does now:**
- **While a server is down:** each server's event stream notices when the server stops answering and when it comes back. The Jobs page then names it above the list ("The Bastion server Two cannot be reached. Its jobs show what was last read.") and keeps that server's jobs, dimmed and marked unreachable.
- **When it comes back:** the note clears and the page reads again, with no reload.
- **A server that answers with an error** still shows the error, as in "local: invocation timed out".

**Checked live:** I killed only Two's server, and the note appeared. I restarted it, and the note cleared and Two's job came back without a reload.

**A mistake of mine, caught by that check:** my first version also hid the error line, so the local server's jobs vanished without a word while its stack was down. The local server was reachable but couldn't read its database. Both lines show now, and a test covers it.

**One limit:** if the page reloads while a server is already down, it has no earlier read of that server's jobs, so it shows only the note.

**Checks:** the 6 page tests pass, clippy is clean, and the CodeScene gate passes.

**Left running:** both stacks are stopped, but the local server still runs.

Next in the plan is A8 step 4 (Build: implement per task, checks, verify, refactor with your pick, acceptance, review with your pick). It now lands in the server.

import re
for p in ['crates/bastion-server/src/store.rs','crates/bastion-server/src/factory/tests.rs']:

        block=m.group(0)

        return re.sub(r'(\n(\s*)branch: [^\n]*,)', r'\1\n\2checks: String::new(),', block, count=1)

    open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

content.text:
I pushed 63eb225, and A8 step 4, the build stages, is committed as 5c18ddf (not pushed).

**What it adds:**
- **Checks per workspace:** each workspace has a checks command, such as `pytest -q`, set in Settings. The checks step runs it in the job's VM:
  - It passes on exit 0.
  - A failure goes back to implement with its output, up to twice.
  - A command that can't run at all waits for you, since no code fix will help.
  - A workspace with no command passes the step.
- **Refactor and code review turns:** provisioning tags the VM `bastion-base`, and both turns diff against it. Each replies with a `REFACTORS:` or `FINDINGS:` list. With nothing listed, the job passes the pick and goes on.
- **The pick pages:** they show the refactor or review report, and the findings pick shows the diff too. You pick by note: approve means "none", and a note names which ones to do. The core then sends that work to implement and back.

**Checks:** 90 core, 79 server, 5 app, 6 page and 1 protocol tests pass. Clippy is clean, the seams hold, and the CodeScene gate passes (`store.rs` improved).

**Not run live:** a job on the full pipeline can't finish until step 5 adds ship. The live check comes with A8's exit.

**A limit:** picking happens by writing a note, not by ticking boxes. Checkboxes would need the report as structured items on the page. That's a small follow-up if you want it.

Next is step 5, ship: commit and push, CI, the CI fix, prove, comprehend, UAT, merge, deploy, learn and teardown, then revive and onboard. Revive also covers the VM a waiting job loses when its stack restarts.

content.text:
Step 5 is big, so I'll split it in two:

- **5a, the ship flow:** ship → CI → CI fix → prove → comprehend → UAT → merge → deploy → learn → landed.
- **5b:** revive and onboard. Each needs a new stage, which means a second store migration, and revive needs a decision about commits that are still only in a lost VM.

The core already moves a job through most of 5a. I'm reading how the short pipeline lands today: the forge, the land, and merging a pull request.

content.text:
Step 5a is committed (ebcc75f), not pushed.

**The ship flow, ship through learn:**
- **Ship:** brings the VM's commits back to the worktree.
  - With the GitHub forge, it pushes and opens the pull request, or reuses it after a CI fix.
  - With the local forge, it passes, and CI is skipped since there is no pull request.
- **CI:** a failure goes through CI fix, then ship again, up to 3 times.
- **Prove:** ends with a `VERDICT:` line. "yes" goes on. "no" sends the work back to implement once. Anything else waits for you, and you can approve or send it back with a note.
- **Comprehend:** writes a short briefing. The UAT page shows it, and the merge page shows it with the diff.
- **Merge:** merges the pull request. With the local forge, it lands into the workspace's branch here.
- **Learn:** proposes rule changes and ends the job.
- **Deploy:** passes. Nothing watches CD yet; the code marks this.

**Checks:** 92 core and 80 server tests pass. Clippy is clean, and the seam check and the CodeScene gate pass. Not run live; the A8 exit covers the full pipeline.

**For 5b, I'd change the scope:**
- **Onboard moves to A9.** A9 already plans onboarding a repository with no settings, and it now fits workspaces on servers better.
- **Revive needs a decision.** When a job's VM is lost, its commits since the last ship are lost too, because they lived only in the VM. My recommendation: after every turn that can change code (implement and CI fix), bring the VM's commits back to the worktree, as ship does. Then revive is always possible: build a new VM from the worktree and go on from the same stage. The cost is one bundle copy per turn, a few seconds each.

Should I do 5b that way?

/// The baseline found checks that pass before anything was built.
+    /// The job's VM is gone, as after its stack restarted. Its commits are
+    /// in the worktree, so a new VM picks the job up where it was (revive).
/// How a checkpoint is decided (D15): the owner decides, the default lands
(State::NeedsYou, event) if decides(&next, event, dials) => approved(&mut next, dials),
(State::NeedsYou, Event::Commented { text }) => commented(&mut next, text, dials),
(_, event) if next.stage == Stage::Land => match land(&mut next, event, dials) {
+/// How many times in a row a job may lose its VM before it fails.
+/// Give the job a new VM, which re-enters its stage once provisioned. A VM
+/// that keeps dying fails the job rather than looping.
+        return fail(job, "the job's VM was lost again after a revive");

content.text:
Step 5b, revive, is committed as a0325d1. It's not pushed, and neither is 5a (ebcc75f).

**How revive works:**
- **Commits kept on the host:** after every turn that writes code (build, implement, CI fix, specify), its commits come back to the job's worktree, so a lost VM loses none of them.
- **Noticing a lost VM:** the sandbox answers `sandbox not found` at a turn's start, a step or a land. The job then gets a new VM on the same worktree and re-enters the stage it was in. If the VM is lost more than twice in a row, the job fails rather than looping.
- **The diff base survives:** provisioning now tags `bastion-base` at the commit where the job forked from its workspace's branch. A revived VM therefore still diffs against where the job began, not against its own commits.

**Lost in a revive:** work a turn left uncommitted, and the `bastion-spec` tag. Without the tag, verify waits for you after a revive.

**Onboarding** moved to A9 in the plan.

**Checks:**
- 93 core, 81 server, 5 app, 6 page and 1 protocol tests pass. A new server test shows that revive keeps the worktree, creates one new VM per revive, and fails the job on the third loss.
- Clippy is clean, the seams hold, and the CodeScene gate passes; `turn_done` went from complexity 11 down to 9.

**Disk:** the disk filled up again mid-build, with 166 MB free. I deleted the incremental compile cache (6.4 GB), and 4 GB is free now. The whole disk is 98% used, so this will keep happening. Freeing space outside the repository would help.

Next in A8: step 6 (split a request into dependent parts), step 7 (pick the pipeline per request and set a dial per checkpoint in Settings), then the A8 exit, live.

(eval):1: no matches found: --include=*.md
## 2. Non-goals

- Not an editor or a file browser. The diff artifact is the only view of code.
  "Open in editor" hands a worktree path to the owner's own editor.
- Not an agent chat. The owner talks to a job through its artifacts and
  checkpoints, not through a prompt box per agent.
- Not a browser app, and no HTTP API.
- Not multi-user. One owner, on their own machine. No sign-in. This drops
  wipp's accounts, GitHub sign-in, org check and roles (§7.1).
- Not a new agent runtime. Turns run on the stock `harness`, `llm-router` and
  `iii-sandbox` workers.
- Not hosted. wipp runs on Fly for a GitHub org, behind Caddy. Bastion runs
  on the owner's machine, so the Fly deploy is not ported (§7.1).
- Not a remote client yet. The owner's box is §10.
- Not Windows. Sandbox VMs need Apple Silicon or Linux with `/dev/kvm`.

## 3. Fixed decisions

content.content:
# Bastion

Bastion is a software factory that runs on your own machine. A request goes in,
agents work it through a pipeline of stages, and a reviewed change comes out.
Nothing merges itself. It's a native app (Tauri 2, Leptos, Rust) on the
[iii](https://iii.dev) engine, and it's early: the app shell, Doctor and the
stack controls work, and the factory itself starts in phase A3 of
[PLAN.md](PLAN.md).

```sh
cargo tauri dev
```

That opens the app. Go to **Engine**, press **Start**, and Bastion runs Doctor,
then brings up the stack in `worker-compose.yaml`. If the stack already runs,
the app attaches to it instead of starting a second one.

## What it is not

Not an editor: the only code you see in Bastion is the diff a job proposes. Not
a web app, and it serves no HTTP. Not multi-user: one owner, no sign-in. Not
Windows, because sandbox VMs need Apple Silicon or Linux with `/dev/kvm`.

## What you need

- Rust, from `rust-toolchain.toml` (rustup picks it up), and the
  `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target.
- `cargo install tauri-cli trunk`.
- `iii` 0.25.0 on your `PATH`.
- A model provider key, such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `OPENAI_API_KEY`, in the
  environment you start Bastion from. The stack inherits it.
- `gh`, signed in, for pushes and pull requests. Landing locally works
  without it.

If something is missing, Doctor on the Engine page names it and says how to
fix it. A failed required check stops the start.

## How it fits together

| Part | Where | Does |

content.thinking: The screenshot's text isn't in this repo, but the same two statements appear in PLAN.md and README.md, and the "no HTTP API" non-goal is already outdated. I need three decisions from you before I plan the shared Bastion server mode.

questions.question: How should people sign in to a shared Bastion server?

options.label: GitHub sign-in (Recommended)
options.description: Sign in with GitHub through the device flow, as wipp did, with an optional org check. People already have the account, the server never stores a password, and a job's pushes and PRs can carry the person's identity. The local server stays signed-in as you with no step.

options.label: Server-issued tokens
options.description: An admin adds a person on the server, which issues them a token to paste into the app (as for Two today). Simplest to build; no outside service; tokens are the only secret, so revoking means deleting one.

options.label: Both
options.description: GitHub sign-in for people, and issued tokens for scripts and CI. Most flexible; about twice the work.

questions.question: What should different people be allowed to do on a shared server?

options.label: Admin and member (Recommended)
options.description: Admins manage the server: its settings, workspaces, constraints, capabilities and people. Members submit requests and act on their own jobs; anyone can see all jobs. Matches wipp's roles closely enough.

options.label: Everyone equal
options.description: Anyone signed in can do anything. Simplest; fits a small trusted team.

options.label: Admin, member and viewer
options.description: Adds read-only people who can watch jobs and the audit log but change nothing.

questions.question: When should this happen in the plan?

options.label: After A8 (Recommended)
options.description: Finish the full pipeline (steps 6 and 7 and the live exit) first, then a new phase for people: sign-in, roles, the actor on every record and audit entry, and serving beyond loopback (TLS or behind a proxy).

options.label: Now, before A8 step 6
options.description: Do people first, so split and the owner's choices are built per person from the start.

**Goal:** several people sign in to one Bastion server, each with a role, and
every record says who did what (D31, D32). It runs between A8 steps 5 and 6,
so split and the owner's choices are built per person.

**Steps:**

- **P1, people in the store.** Migration 2 adds `people` (name, role) and
  `tokens` (the token's SHA-256, its person, a label, when it was made and
  last used). A server's first start makes its admin, named by `--owner` or
  `git config user.name`, with the token in `data/token`.
- **P2, a person on every request.** The token resolves to a person, and each
  route checks the role: a viewer may only read, a member may submit and act
  on their own jobs, an admin may do everything. A refusal is 403 with why.
- **P3, the actor on every record.** A job keeps who requested it, each
  checkpoint who decided it, and each audit entry its actor. The Jobs page
  shows who asked.
- **P4, managing people.** Routes to list people, add one, change a role, and
  issue or revoke a token (shown once). A People section in Settings for
  admins. The page reads who you are on each server and hides what your role
  cannot do.
- **P5, serving beyond loopback.** `--listen <address>` with `--tls-cert` and
  `--tls-key`; without them the server refuses any address but loopback.

viewer. The member's request runs to its first checkpoint and the member
approves it; the viewer sees the job but cannot approve it, and the server
refuses the viewer's attempt with 403; the member cannot change a
constraint, and the admin can. The audit log names each of them.

#### A8 — The full pipeline (L)""")

| S | in progress |""")

Windows, because sandbox VMs need Apple Silicon or Linux with `/dev/kvm`."""

servers over HTTP. It runs locally by default; a shared Bastion server can take
several people, each signing in with a token the server issued them. Not
Windows, because sandbox VMs need Apple Silicon or Linux with `/dev/kvm`.""")
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

input.command:
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -q -- -D warnings 2>&1 | grep -E "^(error|warning)" | head -3; python3 - <<'EOF'
p='PLAN.md'; s=open(p).read()
a="| P | next | Added 2026-11-06 (D31, D32). Runs before A8 step 6. |"
assert a in s
s=s.replace(a,"| P | in progress | Added 2026-11-06 (D31, D32). Runs before A8 step 6. P1 to P3: `bastion_core::people` holds the roles and what each may do; `people` and `tokens` tables keep each person and each token's SHA-256, never the token; a server's first start makes its owner (`--owner`, else `git config user.name`) an admin, and the token in `data/token` is the owner's even before the database opens. Every request resolves its token to a person, and `access` checks the role against what the route does: reads for all, submitting for members and admins, acting on a job for its requester or an admin, everything else for admins; a refusal is 403 with who and why. A job keeps its requester, the Jobs page shows it, and every successful change goes in the audit log as `act` with who made it. `GET /me` says who you are. 94 core, 86 server tests. Next: P4, managing people. |")
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
P1 to P3: people, roles and the actor on every record

A Bastion server keeps its people and each token's SHA-256, never the
token. Its first start makes the owner an admin, and data/token is the
owner's token even before the database opens. Every request resolves its
token to a person, and the role decides: anyone reads, members and admins
submit, a job's requester or an admin acts on it, and admins change the
server. A refusal is 403 with who and why. Jobs keep who asked, the Jobs
page shows it, and each change goes in the audit log with its actor.
EOF
git log --oneline -1

input.prompt:
Research spike for Bastion (repo /Users/tacoda/tacoda/bastion), read-only: do NOT edit repo files, do NOT start or stop any iii stack, do NOT print secret values from the environment.

Context: Bastion runs an iii 0.25.0 stack from worker-compose.yaml with workers `secrets` (0.1.6), `llm-router` (1.4.41), `provider-anthropic` (1.2.29), `provider-openai` (1.2.29). Cached packages are binaries under ~/.iii/compose/packages/ (also provider-deepseek 0.1.20, provider-openai-codex). Today the provider workers get their API keys from the environment (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY) that the stack inherits. The owner wants keys set in Bastion's own configuration instead (no env dependency), for many providers: Anthropic, OpenAI, open-weight models (Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi/Moonshot, GLM/Zhipu) and hosts (Fireworks, Together.ai), ideally anything OpenAI-compatible.

Find out, with evidence (command output, strings from binaries, docs URLs):
1. Which provider worker packages exist in the iii registry. Try the `iii` CLI (e.g. `iii --help`, `iii worker --help`, any search/list/registry subcommand), and https://iii.dev/docs if reachable (use WebFetch/WebSearch if available).
2. For provider-anthropic and provider-openai (and deepseek): how they get credentials. Run `strings` (or grep -a) on the binaries for env var names (e.g. *_API_KEY, *_BASE_URL), for references to the `secrets` worker (function ids like `secrets::get`), and for config keys usable in worker-compose `config_override` (api_key, base_url, models...). Report exact names.
3. Whether provider-openai (or any package) accepts a custom base URL so it can serve OpenAI-compatible hosts (Together, Fireworks, DeepSeek, Moonshot, Zhipu, DashScope/Qwen, OpenRouter). Look for base_url/endpoint strings and how multiple instances could be declared (e.g. two compose entries with different names/configs, `provider-openai#together` style keys like the `iii-worker-manager#governed` entry in worker-compose.yaml).
4. What llm-router exposes for providers/credentials: strings for function ids like `router::provider::*`, `router::*` and anything about registering providers, credentials, or a secrets lookup.
5. What the `secrets` worker exposes (function ids like secrets::set/get/list) and whether providers read from it.

Report under ~600 words: a table of providers available + how each takes its key, the exact env/config/secret names, and your recommendation for how Bastion can let an owner configure keys for these providers without env vars (e.g. write keys into the secrets worker; or write config_override per provider and restart that container; or per-instance compose entries for OpenAI-compatible hosts). Mark anything you inferred rather than saw.
